description:
Team MONOLITH

Team MONOLITH (Lomé, Togo) is building C-Sync, an offline health companion for astronauts on long missions. When Earth is up to 20 minutes away, C-Sync helps the crew check their own health, explains every value against their personal baseline, guides measurements step by step in an emergency, and prepares a clear report for the crew medical officer and flight surgeons. It never diagnoses: the decision stays human.
summary: C-Sync (Care Sync) is an offline-first assistant for a deep-space crew that is minutes or days away from help. It compares each astronaut with their own baseline, flags drifts in body, attention and morale, shows what it does not know as UNKNOWN (never as normal), guides the crew step by step in a medical emergency, and queues the report for the ground. A resume gate refuses to restart work when the supporting measurement is stale, and the final decision always stays with a human. It runs on synthetic crew data labelled as such and on real NASA ISS cabin telemetry for habitat context.
details: C-Sync (Care Sync) works on the crew's side, where a message to Earth can take up to about 22 minutes each way and links can drop for days. It does three things. 1. Notice. Each astronaut is compared with their own baseline (first five days), not a universal norm. An indicator is flagged when it drifts by at least 1.5 standard deviations for two consecutive days; one flag gives WATCH, two or more give DEGRADED, and two dimensions away from baseline open a fatigue procedure. Body, Attention and Morale are evaluated; Mission and Habitat are context. Missing data is shown as UNKNOWN, never as normal. 2. Guide. On an emergency event (in our story, chest pain) it opens a fixed procedure, guides the measurements one by one (how to take each, with a NASA source), records each value with its time and origin, and queues the report for the ground; the queue delivers it once, without duplicates. It proposes no treatment and no drug; a fixed sentence points to the onboard medical checklist and the crew medical officer. 3. Protect the decision. A resume gate refuses to resume work when the last measurement is older than 10 minutes and explains why in plain words. A commander override is logged but never sufficient on its own. The app also has a Commander board (the same rule on six synthetic crew members, sorted by urgency, deciding nothing), a body map with eight zones, trend charts, a habitat panel with real NASA data, and a reader for a text format of device measurements (format check only; no real device is connected). Evidence: on synthetic crews, with the rule never retuned on them, 0 of 300 healthy crews triggered a procedure (2.0 % on a second set of 200, so 0 to 2 % depending on the simulated crews), 139 of 150 gradual drifts (92.7 %) and 86 of 150 abrupt shifts (57.3 %) were detected; the abrupt case is the known weak point. Crew data is synthetic (generator csync-synth-0.1, labelled with version and seed). Nothing is clinically validated. Stack: Python, NumPy, pandas, Streamlit, jsonschema, pytest (211 tests). Next steps: expert review of the rules, then a trial on analog-isolation data, then real sensors. Demo: 7 slides (English) at the Project Demonstration link. Full AI declaration, sources and licences are in AI_USAGE.md and SOURCES.md in the repository.
